title: When God Sent a Lying Spirit — 1 Kings 22:19–23
paragraphs: When God Sent a Lying Spirit — 1 Kings 22:19–23
Heaven’s throne was not trembling.
Ahab’s was.

In one of the most unsettling scenes in Scripture, the prophet Micaiah says he saw the Lord on His throne, with the host of heaven standing beside Him, and a spirit stepping forward to entice King Ahab through the mouths of false prophets. Read it slowly. It is shocking on purpose. God was not deceived. Ahab was being handed over to the deception he already loved.
That is the terror of a hardened heart.
A man can reject truth so long that judgment arrives wearing the clothes of his own desires.

Ahab did not want God’s word. He wanted approval. He gathered prophets, not for repentance, but for validation. He wanted a sermon that fit his appetite. And when Micaiah finally spoke the truth, Ahab hated the truth more than the lie. That is why 1 Kings 22 is so heavy. The lying spirit did not create Ahab’s rebellion. It exposed it.
But here’s what we miss.

This passage is not telling us that God becomes sinful. Scripture is clear: God does not lie, and He is never the author of evil in the moral sense. He is holy, just, and utterly pure. In this scene, God is acting as Judge over a king who has repeatedly despised the truth. Some scholars interpret this as God judicially permitting deception as an act of judgment on someone who has persistently rejected His word. That fits the wider biblical pattern: when people stubbornly suppress truth, God may give them over to what they insist on having.
That should make us tremble.
Because the scariest judgment is not thunder.
It is being left alone with the lie you begged to keep.

And yet this story does not end as a warning only. It points us to our need for a better King and a better word. Where Ahab surrounded himself with flattering voices, Jesus is the true King who always speaks truth, even when it wounds before it heals. Where false prophets led a man to death, Christ took death upon Himself so liars, rebels, hypocrites, and truth-runners like us could be forgiven.
This is the Gospel.

We have all loved convenient lies. We have all edited God’s voice to protect our idols. But Jesus came full of grace and truth. He does not flatter sinners. He saves them. At the cross, truth named our sin. And grace bore our punishment. In the resurrection, Christ shattered the final lie that judgment is the end for all who repent and believe.
So do not play with deception.
Do not build your life on voices that only tell you what you want to hear.
Run to the Word. Run to Christ. Ask God for a heart that loves truth more than comfort. Because the same God who judged Ahab now offers mercy to all who bow to His Son.
No matter how long you have listened to lies, Jesus can retrain your ears.
No matter how far deception has dragged you, grace still speaks louder.
